source_text: Sit ergo nostri operis exordium quaestio illa consequens ac secunda, utrum potestate unius dei mundus regatur anne multorum. nemo, qui quidem sapiat rationemque secum putet, non unum esse intellegat, qui et condiderit omnia et eadem qua condidit uirtute moderetur. quid enim multis opus est ad mundi regimen sustinendum? nisi forte arbitrabimur, si plures sint, minus habere singulos neruorum atque uirium: quod quidem faciunt ii qui esse multos uolunt, quia necesse est inbecillos esse, siquidem singuli sine auxilio reliquorum tantae molis gubernaculum sustinere non possunt. deus autem, qui est aeterna mens, ex omni utique parte perfectae consummataeque uirtutis est: quod si uerum est, unus sit necesse est. potestas enim uel uirtus absoluta retinet suam propriam firmitatem. id autem solidum existimandum est, cui nihil decedere, id perfectum, cui nihil possit accedere. quis dubitet potentissimum esse regem qui totius orbis habeat imperium? neque inmerito. cum illius sint Quae ubique sunt omnia cum ad eum solum omnes undique copiae congerantur. at si plures partiantur orbem, minus certe opum, minus uiriuni singuli habebunt, cum intra praescriptam portionem se quisque contineat. eodem modo etiam dii, si plures sint, minus ualebunt, aliis tantundem in se habentibus. uirtutis autem perfecta natura in eo potest esse in quo totum est quam in eo in quo pars exigua de toto est. deus uero si perfectus est, ut esse debet, non potest esse nisi unus, ut in eo sint omnia. deorum igitur uirtutes ac potestates infirmiores sint necesse est, quia tantum singulis deerit, quantum in ceteris fuerit: ita quanto plures tanto minores erunt. quid quod summa illa rerum potestas ac diuina uis ne semel quidem diuidi potest? quidquid enim capit diuisionem, et interitum capiat necesse est. si autem interitus procul est a deo, quia incorruptibilis est et aeternus, consequens est ut diuidi potestas diuina non possit. deus ergo unus est, si nihil esse aliut potest quod : tantundem capiat potestatis: et ii tamen qui multos esse arbitrantur officia inter se dicunt esse partitos. de quibus omnibus suo loco disputabimus. illud interim quod ad praesentem locum pertinet teneo: si partiti sunt inter se officia, eodem reuoluitur res, ut ex iis quilibet sufficere omnibus nequeat. perfectus igitur non erit qui cessantibus ceteris non potest omnia gubernare. ita fit ut ad regendum mundum unius perfecta uirtute opus sit quam inbecillitate multorum. qui autem putat hanc tantam magnitudinem non posse ab uno regi, fallitur neque quanta sit uis ac potestas diuinae maiestatis intellegit, si existimat singularem deum qui facere mundum potuit, eundem regere non posse quem fecit. at si concipiat animo quanta sit diuini huius operis inmensitas (eamque) cum antea nihil esset, tamen uirtute atque consilio dei ex nihilo esse conflatam, quod opus nisi ab uno inchoari perficique non potuit, iam intelleget multo facilius esse ab uno regi quod est ab uno constitutum. dicat fortasse aliquis ne tabricari quidem tam inmensum opus mundi nisi a pluribus potuisse. quamlibet multos, quamlibet magnos faciat, quidquid in multis magnitudinis potestatis uirtutis maiestatisque posuerit, id totum in unum confero et in uno esse dico, ut tantum in eo sit istarum rerum, quantum nec cogitari nec dici potest. qua in re quoniam et sensu deficimur et uerbis, quia neque tantam intellegentiae lucem pectus humanum neque explanationem tantarum rerum capit lingua mortalis, id ipsum intellegere nos oportet ac dicere. uideo rursus quid e contrario dici possit, tales esse illos plures qualem nos uolumus unum. at hoc fieri nullo pacto potest, quod singulorum potestas progredi longius non ualebit occurrentibus sibi potestatibus ceterorum. necesse est enim ut suos quisque limites aut transgredi nequeat aut si transgressus fuerit, suis alterum finibus pellat. non uident qui deos multos esse credunt fieri posse ut aliquid diuersum uelint, ex qua re disceptatio inter eos et certamen oriatur; sicut Homerus bellantes inter se deos finxit, cum alii Troiam capi uellent, alii repugnarent. unius igitur arbitrio mundum regi necesse est. nisi enim singularum partium potestas ad unam prouidentiam referatur, non poterit summa ipsa constare, uno quoque nihil curante amplius quam quod ad eum proprie pertinet, sicut ne res quidem militaris nisi unum habeat ducem atque rectorem. quodsi in uno exercitu tot fuerint imperatores quot legiones, quot cohortes, quot cunei, quot alae, primum nec instrui poterit acies uno quoque periculum recusante nec regi facile aut temperari, quod suis propriis consiliis utantur omnes, quorum diuersitate plus noceant quam prosint: sic in hoc rerum naturae imperio nisi unus fuerit ad quem totius summae cura referatur, uniuersa soluentur et conruent. dicere autem multorum arbitrio regi mundum tale est, quale si quis adfirmet in uno corpore multas esse mentes, quoniam multa et uaria sint ministeria membrorum, ut singulos corporis sensus singulae mentes regere credantur, item multi adfectus, quibus commoueri solemus uel ad iram uel ad cupiditatem uel ad laetitiam uel ad metum uel ad miserationem, ut in his omnibus totidem mentes putentur operari. quod si quis profecto dicat, ne ipsam quidem quae una est habere uideatur. quodsi in uno corpore tantarum rerum gubernationem mens una possidet et uniuersis simul intenta est, cur aliquis existimet mundum non posse ab uno regi, a pluribus posse? quod quia intellegunt isti adsertores deorum, ita eos praeesse singulis rebus ac partibus dicunt, ut tamen unus sit rector eximius. iam ergo ceteri non dii erunt, sed satellites ac ministri, quos ille unus maximus ac potens omnium iis officiis praefecerit, ut ipsi eius imperio ac nutibus seruiant. si uniuersi pares non sunt, non igitur dii omnes sunt: nec enim potest hoc idem esse quod seruit et quod dominatur. nam si deus nomen est summae potestatis, incorruptibilis esse debet, perfectus inpassibilis nulli rei subiectus. ergo dii non sunt quos parere um maximo deo necessitas cogit. sed quia non frustra falluntur qui hoc ita putant, causam huius erroris paulo post aperiemus. nunc unitatem diuinae potestatis testimoniis conprobemus.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore let the beginning of our work be that question which follows and is second, whether the world is ruled by the power of one God or of many. No one, who indeed is wise and thinks reason with himself, does not understand that there is one who both founded all things and governs them with the same virtue with which he founded them. For what need is there for many for sustaining the rule of the world? Unless perhaps we might think that if there are more, individual ones have less nerve and strength: which indeed those who want there to be many do, because it is necessary for them to be weak, since individual ones cannot sustain the helm of such a great burden without the help of the rest. But God, who is eternal mind, is perfect and complete virtue in every part: which if it is true, it is necessary for there to be one. For absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness. That which is solid is to be thought of as that to which nothing can be lacking, that which is perfect is that to which nothing can be added. Who would doubt that the most powerful king is he who has dominion over the whole world? And not without reason. For all things that are everywhere are his, and all resources from everywhere are gathered to him alone. But if many divide the world, individual ones will certainly have less wealth, less strength, since each one is contained within his own prescribed portion. In the same way also, if there are many gods, they will be less powerful, having as much in themselves as others have. The perfect nature of virtue can be in that in which the whole is, rather than in that in which a small part of the whole is. But if God is perfect, as he ought to be, he cannot be anything but one, so that all things may be in him. Therefore the virtues and powers of the gods must be weaker, because as much is lacking to individual ones as is in the others: so the more there are, the smaller they will be. What of the fact that the highest power of things and divine strength cannot even once be divided? For whatever undergoes division must also undergo destruction. But if destruction is far from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal, it follows that divine power cannot be divided. Therefore God is one, if nothing else can have as much power: and yet those who think there are many say that they have divided offices among themselves. We will dispute about all these things in their own place. Meanwhile I hold this, which pertains to the present topic: if they have divided offices among themselves, the matter comes to the same thing, so that each one cannot suffice for all. Therefore he will not be perfect who cannot govern all things with the rest ceasing. So it happens that for ruling the world the perfect virtue of one is needed, rather than the weakness of many. But he who thinks that this great magnitude cannot be ruled by one is mistaken, and does not understand how great the strength and power of divine majesty is, if he thinks that the singular God who could make the world cannot rule what he made. But if he conceives in his mind how great the immensity of this divine work is (and that) with nothing previously existing, nonetheless it was made from nothing by the virtue and counsel of God, which work could not have been begun or completed by anyone but one, then he will understand that it is much easier for it to be ruled by one than it is for it to have been established by one. Perhaps someone will say that not even a work as immense as the world could have been made by anyone but many. Whatever multitude, whatever greatness he may imagine, whatever magnitude of power, virtue, and majesty he may put in many, I bring all that back to one and say that it exists in one, so that there is as much of those things in him as cannot be thought or said. In this matter, since we fail both in sense and in words, because the human breast does not grasp such a great light of understanding, nor does the mortal tongue grasp the explanation of such great things, we ought to understand and say this. I see again what can be said on the contrary, that those many are such as we want the one to be. But this cannot happen in any way, because the power of individual ones will not be able to proceed further, with the powers of the others encountering them. For it is necessary that each one have his own limits, which he cannot transgress, or if he has transgressed, he drives another back with his own boundaries. Those who believe there are many gods do not see that it is possible for them to will something different, from which a dispute and conflict arise; just as Homer fashioned the gods fighting among themselves, when some wanted Troy to be taken, and others resisted. Therefore it is necessary for the world to be ruled by the decision of one. For unless the power of individual parts is referred to one providence, the sum itself will not be able to stand, with each one caring for nothing more than what pertains to him, just as not even a military thing can have more than one leader and ruler. But if in one army there are as many commanders as there are legions, cohorts, wedges, and wings, first the battle line will not be able to be drawn up, with each one refusing danger, nor will it be easy to rule or temper, because all use their own counsel, whose diversity harms more than it helps: so in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole sum is referred, all things will be dissolved and fall. But to say that the world is ruled by the decision of many is like saying that in one body there are many minds, because there are many and varied ministries of the members, so that individual minds are believed to rule individual senses of the body, and also many affections, by which we are moved either to anger or to desire or to joy or to fear or to pity, so that in all these things as many minds as there are are thought to operate. Which if someone indeed says, he does not even seem to have the one that is. But if in one body one mind possesses the governance of so many things and is attentive to all at the same time, why does someone think that the world cannot be ruled by one, but can be by many? Because those who assert the gods understand this, they say that they preside over individual things and parts, so that nonetheless there is one excellent ruler. Now therefore the rest will not be gods, but satellites and ministers, whom that one greatest and most powerful of all has placed over those offices, so that they serve his command and nods. If all are not equal, therefore they are not all gods: for it cannot be the same thing that serves and that dominates. For if God is the name of the highest power, he ought to be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to no thing. Therefore those are not gods whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God. But because those who think this are not mistaken in vain, we will reveal the cause of this error a little later. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

choices.why: to maintain the unity of divine power
to explain the diversity of the world
to emphasize the uniqueness of God

pass_b_english: Let the starting point of our work, then, be the next question in order: whether the world is ruled by the power of one God or of many. No one who is truly wise and exercises reason fails to understand that there is a single Being who both founded all things and governs them with the very same power by which he created them. What need could there be for many to sustain the government of the world? One might suppose that if there were several, each would possess less strength and force; but that is exactly what proponents of many gods must claim, because if each cannot bear the helm of so vast a burden without the help of the others, they are necessarily weak. God, however, is eternal Mind, perfect and complete in virtue from every angle. If that is true, he must be one. Absolute power or virtue retains its own firmness; what is solid lacks nothing, and what is perfect admits no addition. Who would doubt that the mightiest king is the one who holds dominion over the whole world? And not without reason: all things everywhere belong to him, and all resources from every quarter flow to him alone. If many were to divide the world, each would certainly command less wealth and less strength, confined within a prescribed portion. The same holds for gods: if there are many, they are less powerful, since each has only as much as the others. The perfect nature of virtue can reside only in that which contains the whole, not in that which holds a mere fragment. Since God is perfect, as he must be, he cannot be anything but one, so that all things may be in him. Consequently, the virtues and powers of many gods would have to be weaker, because each lacks exactly as much as the others possess; the more there are, the smaller each becomes. Moreover, the supreme power of reality and divine strength cannot be divided even once. Whatever undergoes division must also undergo destruction. But destruction is remote from God, because he is incorruptible and eternal; therefore divine power cannot be divided. God is therefore one, since nothing else can possess equal power. Yet those who posit many gods claim that they have divided offices among themselves. We will debate all those claims in their proper place. For now I hold to the point at hand: if they have divided offices, the result is the same—no single one can suffice for all. Hence the one who cannot govern all things when the rest cease to act is not perfect. It follows that the world requires the perfect virtue of one, not the weakness of many. Anyone who thinks this vast magnitude cannot be ruled by a single being is mistaken and fails to grasp the greatness of divine strength and majesty. If the one God could make the world, he can certainly rule what he made. Consider the immensity of this divine work: though nothing existed before, it was brought into being from nothing by God's virtue and counsel—a work that could not have been begun or completed by anyone but one. Once this is grasped, it becomes clear that ruling what one has established is far easier than establishing it in the first place. Someone might object that not even a work as immense as the world could have been fashioned except by many. Let him imagine any multitude, any greatness, any magnitude of power, virtue, and majesty distributed among many; I gather all of it into one and declare that it exists in him, so that he possesses those qualities to a degree that cannot be thought or spoken. In this matter we fail both in perception and in language, because the human heart cannot grasp so great a light of understanding, nor can mortal tongue explain such things; yet we must understand and say this much. I see what might be said in opposition: that those many are exactly as we wish the one to be. But that cannot happen in any way, because the power of each cannot advance further when it encounters the powers of the others. Each must have his own limits, which he cannot cross, or if he crosses them he drives another back by his own boundaries. Those who believe in many gods do not see that it is possible for them to will different things, from which dispute and conflict would arise—just as Homer invented gods warring among themselves, some wanting Troy taken, others resisting. Therefore the world must be ruled by the decision of one. Unless the power of individual parts is referred to a single providence, the totality itself cannot hold together, each caring for nothing beyond what pertains to him—just as no military force can have more than one leader and ruler. If a single army had as many commanders as legions, cohorts, wedges, and wings, the battle line could not even be formed, each refusing danger, nor could it be easily directed or controlled, because all would follow their own counsels, whose diversity would harm more than help. So in this command of nature, unless there is one to whom the care of the whole sum is referred, all things will dissolve and collapse. To say the world is ruled by the will of many is like saying that a single body has many minds, because its members have many and varied functions, so that individual minds are thought to govern individual senses, and many affections—anger, desire, joy, fear, pity—are thought to be operated by as many minds. If someone actually says this, he does not even seem to possess the one mind he has. But if one mind in a single body governs so many things and attends to all simultaneously, why would anyone think the world cannot be ruled by one but can be by many? Because the defenders of many gods understand this, they say those gods preside over individual things and parts, yet insist there is still one supreme ruler. Then the rest are not gods at all, but satellites and ministers whom that one greatest and most powerful Being has appointed to those offices, to serve his command and nods. If all are not equal, then they are not all gods; the same thing cannot both serve and rule. If God is the name of the highest power, he must be incorruptible, perfect, impassible, subject to nothing. Therefore those whom necessity compels to obey the greatest God are not gods. But since those who think this way are not mistaken in vain, we will reveal the cause of their error shortly. Now we will confirm the unity of divine power with testimonies.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the nuances of Lactantius's argument regarding divine perfection, the impossibility of division in absolute power, and the analogies of the military and the human body. All clauses in Pass A and B correspond to the Locked Latin.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the argument structure, key terms, and theological distinctions. The passage is complete, and the citations to scripture are not required here as the text does not quote biblical passages. The title 'God's Unity' appropriately captures the central theme of the passage.
